claim: High spliceosome activity is a dependency for cancer cells, making them more vulnerable to perturbation of the splicing machinery compared to normal cells.
source: High spliceosome activity is a dependency for cancer cells, making them more vulnerable to perturbation of the splicing machinery compared to normal cells.
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior work (Koh et al., 2015; Hsu et al., 2015) as indicated in the Introduction section.

claim: Pooled shRNA screens in vitro and in vivo identified HNRNPM as a regulator of prostate cancer cell growth.
source: Our screens identified heterogeneous nuclear ribonucleoprotein M (HNRNPM) as a regulator of PCa cell growth.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data from the shRNA screens described in the Results section.

claim: HNRNPM binding to its targets prevents aberrant exon inclusion and backsplicing events.
source: HNRNPM binding to its targets prevents aberrant exon inclusion and backsplicing events.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and eCLIP data showing increased exon inclusion and circRNA formation upon HNRNPM depletion.

claim: HNRNPM preferentially binds to GU-rich elements in long flanking proximal introns.
source: In both linear and circular mis-spliced transcripts, HNRNPM preferentially binds to GU-rich elements in long flanking proximal introns.
evidence: This is supported by eCLIP data showing HNRNPM binding sites are GU-rich and enriched in long introns flanking mis-spliced exons.

claim: Mimicry of HNRNPM-dependent linear-splicing events using splice-switching-antisense-oligonucleotides was sufficient to inhibit PCa cell growth.
source: Mimicry of HNRNPM-dependent linear-splicing events using splice-switching-antisense-oligonucleotides was sufficient to inhibit PCa cell growth.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing that SSOs inducing HNRNPM-dependent splicing events reduce cell proliferation.

claim: PCa dependence on HNRNPM is likely a result of mis-splicing of key homeostatic coding and non-coding genes.
source: This suggests that PCa dependence on HNRNPM is likely a result of mis-splicing of key homeostatic coding and non-coding genes.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that SSO-induced splicing changes are sufficient to inhibit growth and that HNRNPM regulates splicing of multiple genes in key pathways.

claim: HNRNPM plays a role in supporting cancer cell fitness in other solid tumors beyond prostate cancer.
source: Our results have further been confirmed in other solid tumors.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing HNRNPM depletion inhibits growth in melanoma, lung adenocarcinoma, and pancreatic adenocarcinoma cell lines.

claim: The majority of genes in eukaryotic cells harbor intronic sequences that are removed during RNA splicing and transcript maturation.
source: In eukaryotic cells, the majority of genes harbor intronic sequences that are removed during RNA splicing and transcript maturation (Venter et al., 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Venter et al., 2001.

claim: The spliceosome comprises small non-coding RNAs (U1, U2, U4, U5, and U6), core spliceosomal proteins, and other auxiliary factors.
source: This process is regulated by the spliceosome, comprising small non-coding RNAs (U1, U2, U4, U5, and U6), the core spliceosomal proteins (i.e., U2AF1, U2AF2, SF3B1, etc.), and other auxiliary factors (i.e., HNRNPs, SRSFs, etc.) (Wahl et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Wahl et al., 2009.

claim: Alternative splicing allows cells to regulate gene expression by expressing alternative isoforms of the same gene.
source: By expressing alternative isoforms of the same gene, the cell can regulate both the inclusion/exclusion of specific protein and/or RNA domains (Yang et al., 2016; Ellis et al., 2012) or change transcript half-life (Naro et al., 2017; 't Hoen et al., 2011; Lareau and Brenner, 2015), thus impacting both transcript fate and function.
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Alternative splicing plays a central role in development, cellular differentiation, and cellular response to external or internal stimuli.
source: The regulation of alternative splicing plays a central role in development (Baralle and Giudice, 2017), cellular differentiation (Pimentel et al., 2016), as well as in the cellular response to external or internal stimuli (Shalgi et al., 2014; Hang et al., 2009; Makino et al., 2002; Haque et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Alterations in splicing can confer competitive advantages to cancer cells.
source: However, the same phenotypic plasticity offered by the splicing machinery can work against the cell and organism, and confer competitive advantages to cells under pathological conditions such as cancer.
evidence: This is supported by examples of splicing alterations promoting proliferation, metastasis, and apoptosis avoidance in cancer.

claim: Changes in isoform ratios in cancer may result from mutations in splice sites or in the splicing machinery itself.
source: Some of these changes in isoform ratios may be direct results of mutations in the linear motifs that comprise the splice sites (Puente et al., 2015; Bartram et al., 2017; Jung et al., 2015) or in the splicing machinery itself (Yoshida et al., 2011; Chronic Myeloid Disorders Working Group of the International Cancer Genome Consortium et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2011; Graubert et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Some molecular subtypes of cancer are highly dependent on a functional core spliceosome for survival.
source: In addition to the differential splicing of specific genes, there is also increasing evidence that some molecular subtypes of cancer, which bear mutations in non-splicing-related genes such as MYC, are highly dependent on a functional core spliceosome for survival (Koh et al., 2015; Hsu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Koh et al., 2015 and Hsu et al., 2015.

claim: The pooled shRNA screen utilized a lentiviral library of 520 shRNAs targeting 102 core and auxiliary splicing factors.
source: The screens utilized a lentiviral library of 520 shRNAs targeting 102 core and auxiliary splicing factors, meaning 3–5 shRNAs targeting each gene (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental design.

claim: The screen identified seven genes (HNRNPL, SYNCRIP, HNRNPM, HNRNPF, SF3A1, SRSF2, and SRSF1) that were significantly enriched or depleted in both in vitro and in vivo screens.
source: Using this analysis, we were able to identify a common set of seven genes (HNRNPL, SYNCRIP, HNRNPM, HNRNPF, SF3A1, SRSF2, and SRSF1) that were significantly enriched or depleted in both the in vitro and in vivo screens (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the rotational gene set analysis of the screen data.

claim: The screen identified previously characterized oncogenic splicing factors SRSF1 and HNRNPL, confirming the validity of the screen.
source: These hits included previously characterized oncogenic splicing factors SRSF1 (Karni et al., 2007) and HNRNPL (Fei et al., 2017), further confirming the validity of our screen.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work on SRSF1 and HNRNPL.

claim: Short-term reduced expression of SF3A1, SRSF1, and SRSF2 was rapidly deleterious in normal prostate epithelial cells.
source: Indeed, short-term, reduced expression of several genes, such as SF3A1, SRSF1, and SRSF2, which are essential genes that form part of the core spliceosomal machinery, was rapidly deleterious in the PrECs (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the short-term siRNA screen data in PrECs.

claim: Reduced expression of HNRNPM and HNRNPF mildly affected proliferation in normal prostate epithelial cells, suggesting a long-term oncogenic role rather than an essential role.
source: On the other hand, reduced expression of HNRNPM and HNRNPF mildly affected proliferation in the PrEC line, suggesting a long-term oncogenic role rather than an essential role in PCa (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is supported by the short-term siRNA screen data in PrECs.

claim: Increased expression of HNRNPM correlated with poorer disease-free survival in prostate cancer patients.
source: This analysis correlated with the increased expression of HNRNPM with poorer disease-free survival over time, while this was not the case for HNRNPF (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA PRAD datasets.

claim: HNRNPM mRNA expression levels were significantly higher in tumor samples compared to normal controls in prostate adenocarcinoma patients.
source: Analysis of HNRNPM mRNA expression in normal and tumor prostate adenocarcinoma (PRAD) patient samples in the same datasets suggested that HNRNPM mRNA expression levels were significantly higher in tumor samples when compared with normal controls (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of TCGA PRAD datasets.

claim: HNRNPM protein expression was increased in PCa cells (LNCAP and PC3) but not in normal prostate epithelial cells (PrEC).
source: Western blot analysis of PrEC and PCa cell lines, LNCAP and PC3 further corroborated these observations, showing that protein expression of HNRNPM was increased in PCa cells, but not in normal PrECs (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data.

claim: Reduced HNRNPM mRNA and protein levels in LNCAP cells resulted in reduced cell proliferation.
source: In line with the screen results, reduced HNRNPM mRNA and protein levels in LNCAP cells resulted in reduced cell proliferation (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data.

claim: HNRNPM depletion impairs colony formation in LNCAP cells.
source: Moreover, we showed that HNRNPM depletion impairs colony formation (Figure 2D)
evidence: This is supported by colony formation assay data.

claim: HNRNPM depletion impairs anchorage-independent cell growth in LNCAP cells.
source: and anchorage-independent cell growth (Figure 2E), underscoring a broad role for HNRNPM in preserving cell fitness.
evidence: This is supported by soft agar assay data.

claim: HNRNPM dependency appeared similar in the PC3 PCa cell line, which bears different driver mutations from LNCAP.
source: HNRNPM dependency appeared similar in the PC3 PCa cell line (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B–F), which bears different driver mutations (PTEN null, TP53 null, androgen independent) from LNCAP (PTEN null, TP53 wildtype, androgen dependent) (van Bokhoven et al., 2003).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in PC3 cells and citation to van Bokhoven et al., 2003.

claim: HNRNPM depletion impaired growth in two independently derived human primary PCa cell lines.
source: We were also able to validate our findings in two independently derived human primary PCa cell lines (Figure 2F).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in primary PCa cell lines.

claim: The impact of HNRNPM in PCa is not dependent on specific tumor genotypes or hormone dependency.
source: This suggests that the impact of HNRNPM in PCa is not dependent on specific tumor genotypes or hormone dependency.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that HNRNPM depletion affects multiple PCa cell lines with different genetic backgrounds.

claim: The ability of LNCAP cells to form tumors when xenografted in mice was impaired in HNRNPM-depleted cells compared to control cells.
source: Finally, the ability of LNCAP cells to form tumors when xenografted in mice was impaired in HNRNPM-depleted cells as compared to control cells (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by xenograft tumor growth data.

claim: Tumor growth in xenografted mice correlated to the potency of the shRNA used to deplete HNRNPM.
source: Notably, tumor growth in these mice correlated to the potency of the shRNA used.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that more potent shRNAs resulted in greater tumor growth inhibition.

claim: eCLIP analysis revealed 57,984 high-confidence HNRNPM-bound sites in LNCAP cells spanning 6510 gene bodies.
source: eCLIP analysis (Figure 3—figure supplement 1; eCLIP controls) revealed 57,984 high-confidence (p-value≤0.05, fold enrichment ≥ 1.5) HNRNPM-bound sites in LNCAP cells (Figure 3A, Figure 3—figure supplement 1), spanning 6510 gene bodies.
evidence: This is supported by eCLIP sequencing data.

claim: HNRNPM-bound sites were primarily located in intronic regions of expressed genes (92.3%).
source: These sites were primarily located in intronic regions of expressed genes (92.3%), with very few binding sites found at either intergenic or exonic loci (7.8%; Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by eCLIP data analysis.

claim: Genes bound by HNRNPM were much longer on average compared to all expressed transcripts and non-HNRNPM-bound transcripts.
source: Genes bound by HNRNPM were surprisingly much longer on average (p<2.2e-16; Figure 3C), with median lengths of 4181 bp, compared to the median lengths of 2988 bp for all expressed transcripts and 2447 bp for non-HNRNPM-bound and -expressed transcripts.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of eCLIP data.

claim: HNRNPM-bound sites tended to be guanidine and uridine (GU)-rich.
source: HNRNPM-bound sites tended to be guanidine and uridine (GU)-rich (Figure 3D, E)
evidence: This is supported by nucleotide frequency analysis of eCLIP peaks.

claim: Motif analyses of HNRNPM-bound sites revealed sequences consisting of single or double G residues interspersed with one to two U residues.
source: and motif analyses of these sites revealed sequences consisting of single or double G residues interspersed with one to two U residues (Figure 3E).
evidence: This is supported by motif analysis of eCLIP data.

claim: Only 0.58% of HNRNPM-bound RNAs varied significantly in expression levels during HNRNPM depletion.
source: Expression analyses revealed that (Venter et al., 2001) only 0.58% (38 of 6510 mapped and bound genes) of HNRNPM-bound RNAs varied significantly (p<0.05, FDR < 0.05, fold change ≥ 2 in both shRNA conditions) in expression levels during HNRNPM depletion in either knockdown condition (Figure 4—source data 2)
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: A minority (19.04%) of transcripts that were significantly altered in expression during HNRNPM knockdown were also bound by HNRNPM.
source: and that (Wahl et al., 2009) a minority (19.04%; 38 of 189 differentially and significantly expressed) of transcripts that were significantly altered in expression during HNRNPM knockdown were also bound by HNRNPM (Figure 4A, Figure 4—source data 2).
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and eCLIP data analysis.

claim: The majority of transcript abundance changes occurring in HNRNPM-depleted cells were not likely to be a direct consequence of HNRNPM depletion.
source: These data suggested that the majority of transcript abundance changes occurring in these cells were not likely to be a direct consequence of HNRNPM depletion.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that most differentially expressed transcripts are not bound by HNRNPM.

claim: The majority of significant splicing events affected by HNRNPM loss were increased inclusion of cassette exons.
source: These analyses revealed that the majority of significant splicing events affected by HNRNPM loss (p<0.05, FDR < 0.05, ∆PSI > 0.2) were the increased inclusion of cassette exons (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by splicing analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: A core group of 135 skipped exon events were present and significantly altered in both HNRNPM knockdown conditions.
source: We found a core group of 135 SE events that were present and significantly altered in both HNRNPM KD/shRNA conditions.
evidence: This is supported by splicing analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: 110 (81.5%) of the core 135 identified skipped exon events were found in genes that were bound by HNRNPM.
source: 110 (81.5%) of the core 135 identified events were found in genes that were bound by HNRNPM (Figure 4C, Figure 4—source data 3).
evidence: This is supported by integration of RNA-seq and eCLIP data.

claim: Of the 110 skipped exon events in HNRNPM-bound genes, 96 (87.3%) were events where the cassette exon displayed increased inclusion.
source: Of these 110 events, 96 (87.3%) were events where the cassette exon displayed increased inclusion (lower-left quadrant, Figure 4C).
evidence: This is supported by splicing analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The majority of splicing changes occurring in HNRNPM-depleted cells were highly likely to be a direct consequence of reduced HNRNPM binding.
source: Taken together, these data suggested that the majority of splicing changes occurring in HNRNPM-depleted cells were highly likely to be a direct consequence of reduced HNRNPM binding
evidence: This is inferred from the high overlap between HNRNPM-bound genes and genes with splicing changes.

claim: HNRNPM depletion tends to result in increased exon inclusion.
source: and that HNRNPM depletion tends to result in increased exon inclusion.
evidence: This is supported by the observation that most splicing changes involve increased exon inclusion.

claim: HNRNPM-silenced exons in linear transcripts were flanked by introns that were significantly longer than other introns in the same transcripts, introns flanking other alternatively spliced exons, or introns in all expressed genes.
source: HNRNPM-silenced exons in linear transcripts were flanked by introns that were significantly longer (median: 3024 bp; Figure 4E) than other introns in the same transcripts (median: 1826 bp), introns flanking other alternatively spliced exons (median: 2042 bp), or introns in all expressed genes (median: 1728 bp).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of intron lengths in RNA-seq and eCLIP data.

claim: HNRNPM-binding sites were preferentially found in introns flanking mis-spliced exons compared to other introns of the same transcript.
source: HNRNPM-binding sites were also preferentially found in these introns compared to other introns of the same transcript (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of HNRNPM-binding site distribution in eCLIP data.

claim: Target exons appeared to bear weaker 5′ and 3′ splice sites compared to original flanking splice sites.
source: Target exons appeared to bear weaker 5′ and 3′ splice sites compared to original flanking splice sites (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is supported by splice site strength analysis.

claim: HNRNPM is enriched in the long proximal introns of mis-spliced exons.
source: Overall, we can conclude that HNRNPM is enriched in the long proximal introns of mis-spliced exons.
evidence: This is inferred from the observations about intron length and HNRNPM-binding site distribution.

claim: A total of 1357 circularized transcripts were identified in LNCAP cells.
source: We identified a total of 1357 circularized transcripts in LNCAP cells
evidence: This is supported by circRNA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: 332 circRNAs showed significantly altered expression upon HNRNPM depletion.
source: amongst which 332 circRNAs showed significantly altered expression.
evidence: This is supported by circRNA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: More circRNAs (230/332) were upregulated in HNRNPM-deficient cells, suggesting that HNRNPM typically inhibits the formation of these RNAs.
source: More circRNAs (230/332) were upregulated in HNRNPM-deficient cells, suggesting that HNRNPM typically inhibits the formation of these RNAs (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by circRNA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The vast majority of differentially expressed circRNAs (94%; 312/332) were multi-exonic.
source: The vast majority of these circRNAs (94%; 312/332) were multi-exonic (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is supported by circRNA analysis of RNA-seq data.

claim: The majority (89%; 294/332) of transcripts with changes in backsplicing were bound by HNRNPM.
source: Similar to our observations for the linear-splicing events, we also observed that the majority (89%; 294/332) of transcripts with changes in backsplicing were bound by HNRNPM (Figure 5A)
evidence: This is supported by integration of circRNA and eCLIP data.

claim: The differences in backsplicing frequency observed in HNRNPM-depleted cells are likely to be a direct consequence of reduced HNRNPM binding.
source: suggesting that the differences in backsplicing frequency observed in HNRNPM-depleted cells are likely to be a direct consequence of reduced HNRNPM binding.
evidence: This is inferred from the high overlap between HNRNPM-bound genes and genes with circRNA changes.

claim: Introns flanking HNRNPM-silenced circularizing exons were significantly longer than other introns in the same transcripts or across introns flanking other circRNAs.
source: Similar to linear transcripts, introns flanking HNRNPM-silenced circularizing exons (median: 15.3 kb) were significantly longer than other introns (median: 2.5 kb) in the same transcripts or across introns flanking other circRNAs (median: 13.2 kb; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of intron lengths in circRNA and eCLIP data.

claim: HNRNPM-binding sites were enriched in the proximal 5′ and 3′ introns flanking differentially circularized exons.
source: HNRNPM-binding sites were also enriched in the proximal 5′ and 3′ introns flanking differentially circularized exons. Fewer HNRNPM-binding sites were found in distal introns or introns within the circularized transcripts (Figure 5F).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of HNRNPM-binding site distribution in eCLIP data.

claim: HNRNPM-dependent backspliced exons bore stronger 5′ splice sites than that of the original flanking proximal exons.
source: However, HNRNPM-dependent backspliced exons bore stronger 5′ splice sites than that of the original flanking proximal exons (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is supported by splice site strength analysis.

claim: CircRNAs regulated by HNRNPM had few miRNA binding sites, suggesting that they were not likely to perform as miRNA sponges.
source: CircRNAs regulated by HNRNPM had few miRNA binding sites, suggesting that they were not likely to perform as miRNA sponges because most of them contained only 1–2 common miRNA response elements (MREs; Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of miRNA response elements in circRNAs.

claim: The majority of HNRNPM-dependent circRNAs (231/294) were predicted to have coding potential.
source: The majority of HNRNPM-dependent circRNAs (231/294) were however predicted to have coding potential (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is supported by computational prediction of coding potential.

claim: 294 of the HNRNPM-regulated circRNAs were found expressed in prostate cancer patients.
source: 294 of the HNRNPM-regulated circRNAs were found expressed in patients.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of patient circRNA expression data from Chen et al., 2019.

claim: Expression of HNRNPM-regulated circRNAs was correlated with HNRNPM expression in patients.
source: Expression of these circRNAs was also correlated with HNRNPM expression.
evidence: This is supported by analysis of patient data.

claim: Patients that expressed higher numbers of HNRNPM-regulated circRNAs had significantly lower levels of HNRNPM.
source: Indeed, patients that had expressed higher numbers of these circRNAs had significantly lower levels of HNRNPM (Figure 5I).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of patient data.

claim: Low expression of a cluster of HNRNPM-regulated circRNAs was significantly correlated with increased risk for patient biochemical relapse.
source: Interestingly, low expression of a cluster of HNRNPM-regulated circRNAs was significantly correlated with increased risk for patient biochemical relapse (BCR) (Figure 5J and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis of patient data.

claim: The correlation between circRNA expression and biochemical relapse was not likely to be related to gene expression.
source: This was not likely to be related to gene expression as we did not observe similar effects when patients were stratified by total expression levels of the same genes (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of survival analyses based on circRNA vs. gene expression.

claim: Introduction of an HNRNPM-binding site to a splicing reporter resulted in increased dsRed expression compared to the empty vector control.
source: Flow cytometry analysis of 293T cells transfected with either reporter showed that introduction of an HNRNPM-binding site to the reporter resulted in increased dsRed expression as compared to the empty vector control (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by splicing reporter assay data.

claim: The presence of a HNRNPM-binding site in the reporter was sufficient to cause exon skipping.
source: This suggests that, as predicted, the presence of a HNRNPM-binding site in the reporter was sufficient to cause exon skipping.
evidence: This is inferred from the splicing reporter assay results.

claim: Mutation of the HNRNPM-binding sites in the reporter resulted in increased GFP expression.
source: Conversely, mutation of the HNRNPM-binding sites in the reporter resulted in increased GFP expression (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C, right panels).
evidence: This is supported by splicing reporter assay data.

claim: The presence of HNRNPM is required to suppress exon inclusion in cells.
source: Taken together, these data add support for our observations that the presence of HNRNPM is indeed required to suppress exon inclusion in cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the splicing reporter assay results.

claim: Approximately 43.7% of HNRNPM-bound peaks across the transcriptome were associated with at least one class of repetitive element.
source: Approximately 43.7% of HNRNPM-bound peaks across the transcriptome were associated with at least one class of repetitive element (LINE, SINE, repetitive DNA, or long terminal repeats [LTR]) (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A; all binding sites; bottom panel).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of eCLIP data and repetitive element annotations.

claim: 54.1% and 50.5% of HNRNPM-binding sites found within the proximal flanking introns of mis-spliced exons in linear and circular transcripts intersected with repetitive elements.
source: In contrast, 54.1 and 50.5% of HNRNPM-binding sites found within the proximal flanking introns of mis-spliced exons in linear and circular transcripts intersected with such elements (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A; top left and middle panels).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of eCLIP data and repetitive element annotations.

claim: L1 LINEs represented the major class of repeats that HNRNPM peaks were associated with.
source: Consistent with previous observations, L1 LINEs represented the major class of repeats that HNRNPM peaks were associated with (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B; Kelley et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of eCLIP data and citation to Kelley et al., 2014.

claim: In linear transcripts, there was an increased incidence of potential GQ-forming sequences per kb of intron length in the intron upstream of the mis-splicing events compared to other introns in the same transcript.
source: In linear transcripts, we observed an increased incidence of potential GQ-forming sequences per kb of intron length in the intron upstream of the mis-splicing events (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C; left panel) compared to other introns in the same transcript.
evidence: This is supported by computational prediction of G-quadruplex-forming sequences.

claim: Potential GQ structures were enriched in both the upstream (−1) and downstream (+1) introns flanking mis-spliced circRNA events.
source: In contrast, potential GQ structures were enriched in both the upstream (−1) and downstream (+1) introns flanking mis-spliced circRNA events (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C; right panel).
evidence: This is supported by computational prediction of G-quadruplex-forming sequences.

claim: Several HNRNPM-bound sequences had the capability to form tertiary GQ structures.
source: Using this assay, we were also able to confirm that several HNRNPM-bound sequences had the capability to form tertiary GQ structures (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is supported by hemin-based G-quadruplex assay data.

claim: DMS-MaP sequencing revealed the presence of many local structures at and around HNRNPM-binding sites.
source: Examination of local secondary structure (±1 kb) by DMS-MaP sequencing around representative HNRNPM-binding peaks in the flanking introns of five mis-splicing events in GMPR2, PRKAB2, USP33, ZNF548, and ZNF304 also revealed the presence of many local structures at and around HNRNPM-binding sites (Figure 6—figure supplement 2E–G).
evidence: This is supported by DMS-MaP sequencing data.

claim: Formation of local RNA secondary structures did not appear to be HNRNPM-dependent.
source: Formation of these structures however did not appear to be HNRNPM-dependent (Figure 6—figure supplement 2G).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of DMS-MaP data in control and HNRNPM-depleted cells.

claim: Most HNRNPM-regulated genes are involved in specific key cellular processes including histone lysine methylation and regulation of microtubule polymerization.
source: Gene ontology analysis of these genes suggested that most of these genes are involved in specific key cellular processes (Figure 6B), including histone lysine methylation and the regulation of microtubule polymerization.
evidence: This is supported by gene ontology analysis of mis-spliced genes.

claim: The majority of HNRNPM-dependent linear-splicing events were predicted to result in nonsense-mediated decay or alternative reading frames in their target protein.
source: The majority of HNRNPM-dependent linear-splicing events were predicted to result in nonsense-mediated decay (NMD) or alternative reading frames in their target protein (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A)
evidence: This is supported by computational prediction of splicing outcomes.

claim: The functions or protein levels of many HNRNPM targets were likely to be altered in HNRNPMlow cells.
source: suggesting that the functions or protein levels of many of these targets were likely to be altered in HNRNPMlow cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the predicted splicing outcomes.

claim: Transfection of SSOs targeting splicing events occurring in EED, PRKAB2, and ZNF548 recapitulated splicing events occurring in HNRNPM-deficient cells and led to the loss of cell viability.
source: Transfection of SSOs targeting splicing events occurring in EED, PRKAB2, and ZNF548 recapitulated splicing events occurring in HNRNPM-deficient cells (Figure 6C) and led to the loss of cell viability in target cells.
evidence: This is supported by SSO transfection and cell viability assay data.

claim: Patients that expressed more HNRNPM-regulated exons at PSI higher than the population median had significant survival benefit over those who expressed less.
source: We found that patients that expressed more HNRNPM-regulated exons at PSI higher than the population median had significant survival benefit over those who expressed less (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis of TCGA patient data.

claim: The reduction in cell growth in HNRNPM-deficient cells is likely a result of perturbing multiple genes across different pathways, rather than from a single target.
source: Overall, these results suggest that the reduction in cell growth in HNRNPM-deficient cells is likely a result of perturbing multiple genes across different pathways, rather than from a single target.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that multiple SSOs targeting different genes reduce cell growth.

claim: Loss of HNRNPM expression resulted in increased inclusion of EED exon 10, resulting in a 25-amino acid added in-frame to the EED protein.
source: Loss of HNRNPM expression resulted in increased inclusion of EED exon 10, resulting in a 25-amino acid added in-frame to the EED protein.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq and RT-PCR data.

claim: Addition of the peptide sequence into the EED structure results in disruption of hydrogen bonding within the beta sheet of WD repeat 5.
source: We found that addition of the peptide sequence into the structure results in disruption of hydrogen bonding within the beta sheet of WD repeat 5 (Figure 6E, F, Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling of the EED protein.

claim: Disruption of the WD repeat in EED is likely to disrupt the stability of the WD repeat and affect EED function.
source: This is likely to disrupt the stability of the WD repeat and affect EED function.
evidence: This is inferred from the structural modeling results.

claim: Induction of the specific isoform of EED in LNCAP cells is correlated with reduced H3K27me3 activity.
source: In support of this, we find that induction of this specific isoform of EED in LNCAP cells is correlated with reduced H3K27me3 activity (Figure 6G, Figure 6—figure supplement 3C).
evidence: This is supported by western blot data showing reduced H3K27me3 upon SSO-induced EED exon inclusion.

claim: Loss of EED function is likely to contribute to the reduced proliferation observed upon HNRNPM depletion.
source: These results suggest that loss of EED function is likely to contribute to the reduced proliferation we observed upon HNRNPM.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that EED mis-splicing reduces H3K27me3 and that SSO-induced EED mis-splicing reduces cell growth.

claim: Patients with reduced EED expression have improved disease-free survival compared to patients with high EED expression.
source: Indeed, analyses of the TCGA datasets suggest that patients with reduced EED expression have improved disease-free survival compared to patients with high EED expression (Figure 6H).
evidence: This is supported by survival analysis of TCGA patient data.

claim: HNRNPM loss resulted in growth inhibition in Calu-3, Panc-1, SKMEL147, and MEL501 cell lines representing lung adenocarcinoma, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, and melanoma.
source: Assays conducted in Calu-3, Panc-1, SKMEL147, and MEL501 cell lines, representing lung adenocarcinoma, pancreatic adenocarcinoma, and melanoma, respectively, showed that HNRNPM loss resulted in growth inhibition (Figure 7A, B)
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation assay data in multiple cancer cell lines.

claim: Loss of HNRNPM in Calu-3, Panc-1, SKMEL147, and MEL501 cell lines resulted in the same mis-splicing event in USP33 and EED in a dosage-dependent manner.
source: In addition, loss of HNRNPM in these four cell lines similarly resulted in the same mis-splicing event in USP33 and EED in a dosage-dependent manner (Figure 7C)
evidence: This is supported by RT-PCR data showing similar splicing changes across cell lines.

claim: HNRNPM similarly regulates splicing events across different cell types.
source: suggesting that HNRNPM similarly regulates splicing events across different cell types.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that similar splicing changes occur in multiple cell types upon HNRNPM depletion.

claim: HNRNPM depletion did not impact viability of HepG2, a hepatoblastoma cell line, despite promoting similar HNRNPM-dependent downstream splicing perturbation.
source: Interestingly, the same assay did not impact viability of HepG2, a hepatoblastoma cell line, despite promoting similar HNRNPM-dependent downstream splicing perturbation (Figure 7A–C, rightmost panels).
evidence: This is supported by cell proliferation and RT-PCR data in HepG2 cells.

claim: The expression of HNRNPM-dependent circRNAs identified in PCa is significantly negatively correlated with HNRNPM expression across 10 different primary melanoma cell lines.
source: We confirmed that the expression of the HNRNPM-dependent circRNAs, which we identified in PCa, is significantly negatively correlated with HNRNPM expression (R = −0.42, p<2.2e-16) across 10 different primary melanoma cell lines (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by analysis of circRNA expression data in melanoma cell lines from Hanniford et al., 2020.

claim: HNRNPM may play an important role in regulating growth across multiple, but not all, cancer types.
source: All in all, our results confirm that HNRNPM may play an important role in regulating growth across multiple, but not all, cancer types.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that HNRNPM depletion affects growth in multiple cancer types but not HepG2.

claim: Cancer cells may be especially vulnerable to disruptions in their splicing machinery compared to normal, untransformed cells.
source: Recent evidence suggests that cancer cells may be especially vulnerable to disruptions in their splicing machinery compared to normal, untransformed cells (Koh et al., 2015; Hsu et al., 2015; Braun et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Cancer cell vulnerability to splicing disruption is thought to be a consequence of increased proliferative rates and transcriptional outputs resulting in 'addiction' to a highly functioning spliceosome.
source: This is thought to be a consequence of the increased proliferative rates and transcriptional outputs of cancer cells, resulting in 'addiction' to a highly functioning spliceosome.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about cancer cell biology.

claim: Splice signatures can vary across different cancers, suggesting that unique or sets of splicing factors may regulate different splicing programs across different cancer types.
source: Despite this, splice signatures can vary across different cancers (Sebestyén et al., 2015), suggesting that unique or sets of splicing factors may regulate different splicing programs across different cancer types.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sebestyén et al., 2015.

claim: The phenotypic manifestation of HNRNPM loss in PCa cells is different from what was previously described in breast cancer cells.
source: Interestingly, the phenotypic manifestation of HNRNPM loss in PCa cells is different from what was previously described. Here we describe a role for HNRNPM in maintaining cell fitness but did not observe changes in cell identity programs in PCa cells. In breast cancer cells, loss of HNRNPM inhibits epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT), but not cell growth (Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by comparison with prior work cited (Xu et al., 2014).

claim: HNRNPM has a context-dependent function in cancer, which might depend on its downstream targets and cell of origin.
source: These data are consistent with a context-dependent function for HNRNPM in cancer, which might depend on its downstream targets and cell of origin.
evidence: This is inferred from the observation that HNRNPM has different effects in different cancer types.

claim: Splicing defects occurring during HNRNPM deficiency primarily involve increased exon inclusion and exon circularization, indicating that HNRNPM normally functions to suppress splice site usage in PCa.
source: Splicing defects occurring during HNRNPM deficiency primarily involve increased exon inclusion and exon circularization, indicating that HNRNPM normally functions to suppress splice site usage in PCa.
evidence: This is supported by RNA-seq data showing increased exon inclusion and circRNA formation upon HNRNPM depletion.

claim: HNRNPM-mediated splicing repression is consistent with previous observations on splicing during HNRNPM loss in other cell types.
source: This is consistent with previous observations on splicing during HNRNPM loss in other cell types (Xu et al., 2014; Huelga et al., 2012; Damianov et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Mis-spliced linear-splicing and circularization events occurring during HNRNPM deficiency are located in exons that are flanked by HNRNPM-bound introns.
source: Our data indicate that mis-spliced linear-splicing and circularization events occurring during HNRNPM deficiency are located in exons that are flanked by HNRNPM-bound introns.
evidence: This is supported by integration of RNA-seq and eCLIP data.

claim: HNRNPM occupancy is much lower in other introns in the same transcripts, suggesting that its recruitment is important for ensuring appropriate splice site selection.
source: HNRNPM occupancy is much lower in other introns in the same transcripts, suggesting that its recruitment is important for ensuring appropriate splice site selection.
evidence: This is supported by eCLIP data showing differential HNRNPM binding across introns.

claim: Members of the hnRNP family of proteins have been shown to be important in ensuring correct splice site selection in target genes.
source: Members of the hnRNP family of proteins have been shown to be important in ensuring correct splice site selection in target genes.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about hnRNP proteins.

claim: hnRNP-mediated splicing repression has been attributed to antagonizing core spliceosomal components and/or splicing enhancer proteins from binding to pre-mRNA, as well as alteration of long-range secondary structure in pre-mRNA.
source: hnRNP-mediated splicing repression has been attributed to several modes of action, including antagonizing core spliceosomal components and/or splicing enhancer proteins from binding to pre-mRNA (Zhu et al., 2001; Mayeda and Krainer, 1992; Mayeda et al., 1993), as well as alteration of long-range secondary structure in pre-mRNA to inhibit/promote alternate splice site usage (Solnick and Lee, 1987; Blanchette and Chabot, 1999; Martinez-Contreras et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: HNRNPM specifically prevents mis-splicing in the context of long genes and is especially enriched in long introns across the genome.
source: Our analyses suggest that HNRNPM specifically prevents mis-splicing in the context of long genes and is especially enriched in long introns across the genome.
evidence: This is supported by eCLIP and RNA-seq data analysis.

claim: Increased intron length has been shown to adversely affect correct splice site selection.
source: Increased intron length has been shown to adversely affect correct splice site selection.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about splicing.

claim: Cryptic splice sites that compete with the original 5′ and 3′ splice sites are more likely to be found within a longer intron.
source: For one, cryptic splice sites that compete with the original 5′ and 3′ splice sites are more likely to be found within a longer intron.
evidence: This is based on logical inference about the relationship between intron length and cryptic splice site occurrence.

claim: Increased intron length extends the delay between RNA polymerase II-dependent synthesis of the 5′ and its associated 3′ splice sites, resulting in a higher probability of RNA secondary and/or tertiary interactions forming to bridge a 5′ss and an incorrect proximal cryptic 3′ss.
source: Secondly, increased intron length extends the delay between RNA polymerase II-dependent synthesis of the 5′ and its associated 3′ splice sites, resulting in a higher probability of RNA secondary and/or tertiary interactions forming to bridge a 5′ss and an incorrect proximal cryptic 3′ss.
evidence: This is based on logical inference about the relationship between intron length and RNA structure formation.

claim: Formation of RNA secondary and tertiary structures has been shown to be partially required for correct splice site selection in long introns.
source: Formation of RNA secondary and tertiary structures has been shown to be partially required for correct splice site selection in long introns (Rogic et al., 2008; Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Rogic et al., 2008 and Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: In vertebrates, large introns bear relatively high densities of repetitive regions that are predicted to form both intra- and inter-intron complementary base pairings.
source: In vertebrates, large introns bear relatively high densities of repetitive regions that are predicted to form both intra- and inter-intron complementary base pairings (Shepard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Shepard et al., 2009.

claim: Competition between complementary sequences has been shown to significantly alter splice site selection in both linear and circular transcripts.
source: Competition between such pairs of complementary sequences has been shown to significantly alter splice site selection in both linear and circular transcripts (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: HNRNPM may be required to regulate the formation or interactions between RNA secondary/tertiary structures at target transcripts in order to maintain correct splice site selection.
source: It may be that HNRNPM is required to regulate the formation or interactions between these structures at such transcripts in order to maintain correct splice site selection.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed enrichment of HNRNPM at repetitive elements and G-quadruplex-forming sequences.

claim: HNRNPM was previously shown to interact with several ATP-dependent RNA helicases.
source: In line with this, HNRNPM was previously shown to interact with several ATP-dependent RNA helicases (Brannan et al., 2016), pointing to a possible association with RNA secondary/tertiary structure.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Brannan et al., 2016.

claim: Long, alternatively spliced genes, bearing elevated intron length to exon length ratios, are highly enriched in pathways associated with cancer and other multi-genic diseases.
source: Finally, it has been previously reported that long, alternatively spliced genes, bearing elevated intron length to exon length ratios, are highly enriched in pathways associated with cancer and other multi-genic diseases (Sahakyan and Balasubramanian, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Sahakyan and Balasubramanian, 2016.

claim: Expression of long genes can be rate-limiting for cell survival and/or function.
source: Because of their lengths, expression of this class of genes can be rate-limiting for cell survival and/or function.
evidence: This is based on logical inference about the relationship between gene length and expression kinetics.

claim: Inhibition of transcription elongation by blocking topoisomerase activity is sufficient to impair expression of long genes.
source: Inhibition of transcription elongation by blocking topoisomerase activity is sufficient to impair their expression (King et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to King et al., 2013.

claim: Expression of long genes may be especially vulnerable to depletion of splicing factors such as HNRNPM.
source: In a similar way, we have shown that expression of these genes may also be especially vulnerable to depletion of splicing factors such as HNRNPM.
evidence: This is supported by the data showing that HNRNPM preferentially regulates splicing in long genes.

claim: Expression of long genes may be modulated through synergistic interactions between inhibitors targeting transcription elongation and splicing factors.
source: One prediction that arises from this observation is that expression of these genes may be modulated through synergistic interactions between inhibitors targeting transcription elongation and splicing factors.
evidence: This is speculative reasoning based on the observed vulnerability of long genes to both transcription and splicing perturbations.

claim: Mutations in the splicing factors SRSF2 and U2AF1 have been shown to impair transcription pause-release and drive R loop formation.
source: Indeed, there is some evidence in the literature pointing towards this. Mutations in the splicing factors SRSF2 and U2AF1 have been shown to impair transcription pause-release and drive R loop formation (Chen et al., 2018), suggesting that these two pathways are intimately linked.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chen et al., 2018.
